clue.text: Scottish angler, elderly one wearing black and white primarily, turned up

indicators.note: what is worn sits on the outside, so the wearer goes inside the clothing letters
in a down clue, turning something up flips it so it reads from bottom to top
primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter of each word counts

parts.note: first letter of black
aged means old, elderly
the Roman numeral for one
first letter of white

explanation.surface: An old Scottish fisherman in a black-and-white outfit shows up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angler' suggests a person fishing, but it is the fish. The wordplay is built bottom-up, so the black-and-white initials end up at the foot and head of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Wide-gab is a Scots dialect name for the anglerfish, the big-mouthed fish that lures prey with a fleshy lure.

clue.text: Around ten I notice Esther's backside is more attractive

indicators.note: a backside is the rear end, so only the last letter of the name is wanted and added on
one thing placed around another encloses it, so these letters wrap the next ones

parts.note: to notice something is to see it
X is the Roman numeral for ten
taken as written
the last letter of Esther

explanation.surface: A cheeky remark comparing Esther's rear to someone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: SEE goes around X and I to make SEXIE; the last letter of Esther completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sexy describes someone sexually appealing, and its comparative form fits a phrase about greater allure.

clue.text: Draw on unknown fabric

parts.note: to draw someone in is to lure them
X is the classic algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Someone sketching on a mysterious piece of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, one piece placed 'on' another sits above it. 'Draw' looks like a sketching verb but means attract.
explanation.definitionFit: Lurex is a trade name for a yarn or cloth woven with shiny metallic thread, popular for sparkly clothing.

clue.text: Shock crew with a sick joke

indicators.note: a shock jolts and disturbs, so the letters are thrown out of their order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tells a tasteless joke and appals the crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' reads as a verb acting on the crew, but it is the signal to rearrange 'crew' and 'a sick'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wisecrack is a quick, smart or flippant remark meant to amuse, which is a kind of gag.

clue.text: Short attractive girl wants to solicit? Desist!

indicators.note: something short has been cut down, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a cutie, minus its last letter
to tout is to solicit custom or business

explanation.surface: A small pretty girl wants to go soliciting, and someone tells her to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: CUTIE loses its E, then TOUT follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal command telling someone to stop doing something annoying at once.

clue.text: Decipher a French prayer found in reference library

parts.note: un is French for a

indicators.note: something found in a place lies inside it, so these letters sit within others

parts.note: the initials of reference library
an Ave Maria, or Hail Mary, is a prayer

explanation.surface: Someone works out a French prayer discovered on the shelves of a reference library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found in reference library' sounds like where the prayer was discovered, but it puts the prayer between two initials. Ave is Latin for hail, the opening of the Hail Mary.
explanation.definitionFit: To unravel a mystery or code is to work it out, untangling it as one would a knot of thread.

clue.text: Judges drink beyond capacity

parts.note: capacity is size or volume
to sup is to drink in small mouthfuls

explanation.surface: Judges drinking far more than they can hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beyond' means coming after, so the drink is placed after capacity, the reverse of the clue's order. 'Judges' looks like a noun for court officials but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To size up a person or situation is to assess or form a view of it, which is to weigh it up.

clue.text: Chinese city, formerly claimed to be exciting

indicators.note: a claim is something said out loud, so what counts is the sound of the word

parts.note: Peking is the older Western name for Beijing

explanation.surface: A fact about the Chinese capital's old name and its supposed excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: Peking was the usual English name for Beijing before pinyin spelling took over; said aloud it matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Piquing curiosity or interest means arousing or stimulating it, so the participle works as stirring up.

clue.text: Political adviser in Luxembourg alive after accident at very high speed

parts.note: Mach 1 is the speed of sound, written MACH I

indicators.note: after an accident things are wrecked and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: L is the international vehicle code for Luxembourg
taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician's aide survives a high-speed crash in Luxembourg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' looks like it places one piece behind another, but 'after accident' is the anagram signal for L plus ALIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat whose book The Prince counselled rulers on gaining and keeping power.

clue.text: French composer reduced tempo as intended

indicators.note: reducing makes something smaller, so the name loses its final letter

parts.note: Léo Delibes, composer of the ballet Coppélia, minus his last letter
tempo is the rate or speed of music

explanation.surface: A French composer slows the tempo on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced tempo' looks like a single musical instruction, but 'reduced' belongs to the composer. Delibes wrote the ballets Coppélia and Sylvia.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deliberate is done on purpose, planned and meant rather than accidental.

clue.text: Quatrain, oddly, rejected in Middle Eastern country

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters run backwards
oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, first, third, fifth and so on

parts.note: letters one, three, five and seven of the word

explanation.surface: A four-line poem turned down in a Middle Eastern country.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters of Quatrain give QARI, which read backwards spell the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Iraq is the Arab republic on the Tigris and Euphrates, with Baghdad as its capital.

clue.text: Guru Angad keeps backing island republic

indicators.note: going backwards means reading the letters from right to left
to keep is to hold within, so the answer lies inside the run of letters

parts.note: the letters sit across the two words, read right to left

explanation.surface: A Sikh guru supporting a small island nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Guru Angad was the second Sikh guru; the answer runs backwards across his title and name.
explanation.definitionFit: Nauru is a tiny independent Pacific island nation, one of the smallest sovereign states in the world.

clue.text: Cleaners and tea ladies

parts.note: char is British slang for tea
ladies are women

explanation.surface: Office cleaners and the ladies who serve tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea ladies' reads as one phrase, but splits into two pieces. Char is British slang for tea, from the Chinese cha.
explanation.definitionFit: A charwoman is a woman hired to clean houses or offices, an old-fashioned word for a domestic cleaner.

clue.text: Frigid oaf moves clumsily like a particular ruminant

indicators.note: clumsy movement stumbles about, so the letters end up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cold lout lumbers about like a cow or camel.
explanation.walkthrough: The ruminant is the giraffe, which chews the cud; the suffix -oid means resembling.
explanation.definitionFit: Giraffoid means resembling a giraffe, and the giraffe is a cud-chewing mammal, a specific ruminant.

clue.text: State prison involved in corrupt activity

indicators.note: something involved in a matter is caught up inside it
corrupt means spoiled or perverted, so the letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written
the can is slang for prison

explanation.surface: A government's jail implicated in corruption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State prison' looks like a single institution; 'State' is the definition alone. The can is American slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Vatican City is the tiny sovereign city-state in Rome governed by the Pope, the smallest independent country.

clue.text: Soviet leader who could make one fall asleep in the auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: to drop off is to fall asleep

explanation.surface: A dull Soviet leader whose speeches sent listeners to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'and drop off' run together sounds like his surname. Yuri Andropov led the USSR from 1982 to 1984.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuri Andropov, former KGB chief, was General Secretary of the Communist Party and head of the USSR briefly.

clue.text: A lot of capital given to Australian musician

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the last letter goes

parts.note: Berlin, the German capital, without its last letter
Oz is slang for Australia or Australian

explanation.surface: A large sum of money handed to a musician from Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money but is a city, Berlin, cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Hector Berlioz was a French Romantic composer, best known for the Symphonie fantastique.

clue.text: James Cagney's opening line shows racial discrimination

parts.note: Jim is a familiar form of James

indicators.note: an opening is the very start, so only the initial letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of Cagney
a row is a line

explanation.surface: The first words spoken by the film star James Cagney reveal racism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening line' looks like the first words of a script; 'opening' takes the C and 'line' is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: Jim Crow laws enforced racial segregation in the American South, so the name stands for systematic racism.

clue.text: Crackpots and nuts defending lawsuit

indicators.note: defenders surround what they protect, so these letters go around the others

parts.note: nut is slang for head
a lawsuit is a court case

explanation.surface: Eccentric people and madmen fighting a lawsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like a second word for crackpots but means heads, which wrap around CASE.
explanation.definitionFit: Headcase is British slang for a mad or eccentric person, someone regarded as unhinged.

clue.text: In the way that this writer's keeping women afloat

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it, so the letters hold another inside

parts.note: as means in the way that, as in 'do as I say'
W is the abbreviation for women
this writer is the setter, I, and the 's is is, giving I'M

explanation.surface: The setter explains how they keep women from sinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter, the usual crossword I, and the apostrophe-s stands for 'is'. 'In the way that' reads as an adverbial phrase but supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Aswim is a literary adjective meaning floating or swimming, like awash or adrift.

clue.text: Gunners in Spielberg thriller about Indian independence

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the title runs backwards
one thing in another is placed within it

parts.note: Jaws is the 1975 Spielberg shark film
RA is the Royal Artillery, the British army's gunners

explanation.surface: Soldiers appearing in a Spielberg film about India's freedom struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About Indian independence' reads as the film's subject, but 'about' turns the title round.
explanation.definitionFit: Swaraj, Hindi for self-rule, was the goal of the Indian movement led by Gandhi against British rule.

clue.text: Kelvin meets Irish singer in African country

parts.note: K is the symbol for kelvin, the unit of temperature
Enya is the Irish singer of Orinoco Flow

explanation.surface: A man called Kelvin meets an Irish singer in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Kelvin looks like a man's name but is the unit of temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenya is the East African republic with Nairobi as its capital, on the Indian Ocean coast.

clue.text: Being possessed of musical tone, I sing

indicators.note: to possess is to hold within, so the letters are held inside the words

parts.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A singer boasts of having a musical voice.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the answer speaking for itself: the voice part says 'I sing'.
explanation.definitionFit: An alto is a voice part or singer of that range, so the clue lets the singer introduce themself.

clue.text: Arachne, out of energy, fell badly causing podiatric problem

indicators.note: when you are out of something you have none left, so that letter is dropped
done badly means done wrong, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: the weaver of Greek myth, with her E removed
taken as written
E is the symbol for energy; this is the letter taken out of the name

explanation.surface: Arachne, exhausted, takes a tumble and hurts her foot.
explanation.walkthrough: Arachne is the weaver turned into a spider in Greek myth. 'Fell badly' sounds like an accident, but 'fell' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A fallen arch is a flattening of the foot's arch, a condition treated by a chiropodist or foot doctor.

clue.text: Not very bright room refurbished nicely? Not half

indicators.note: not half here means lose half of the word, keeping only its first three letters
refurbishing remakes and rearranges, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the first half of nicely

explanation.surface: A dim room that has been nicely redone; 'not half' is British for 'very much so'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not very bright' looks like a room with poor lighting, but describes a dim-witted person. 'Not half' is the British retort meaning 'definitely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Moronic means stupid or idiotic, describing someone of low intelligence.

clue.text: Weird-looking boy dressing very loudly to be "in"

indicators.note: dressing something means clothing it, so these letters wrap around another piece
a weird look is a strange form, so the letters take an odd new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
way is informal for very, as in 'way too much'
f, forte, is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: A boy who dresses very loudly in order to be fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very loudly' looks like fortissimo, FF, but splits: 'very' is WAY and 'loudly' is F.
explanation.definitionFit: By way of works as a preposition meaning in the form or capacity of, as in 'by way of apology'.
